messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alejandro had always thought of himself as a tough guy. Growing up in a rough neighborhood in Brooklyn, he learned to navigate danger and come out on top. But nothing could have prepared him for the night his workplace, a large retail store, was ravaged by a massive fire set intentionally by an arsonist. Alejandro, then 30 years old, was working late that evening when the flames erupted. He narrowly escaped with his life, but the memory of those few moments has haunted him ever since. What frightened him most was not just the physical danger he faced, but the realization that someone could so callously disregard human life. This sense of moral violation still grips Alejandro whenever he sees people misbehaving in public – littering, screaming at each other on the street – it's as if they're rubbing their disrespect for others in his face, and he feels a familiar dread creeping up. Those same memories are triggered by something as seemingly innocuous as walking through a crowded shopping mall. The proximity to strangers' bodies makes him feel like he's back in that burning store, desperate to escape the heat and chaos. His skin crawls at the mere touch of certain textures – specifically, the smooth, cold surface of metal railings, which remind him of the twisted wreckage of escalators he saw as he fled the inferno. When these triggers catch him off guard, Alejandro's mind goes into overdrive. He tries to distract himself by telling himself it didn't happen or wasn't that bad – a coping mechanism that has become increasingly tenuous. But no matter how hard he pushes the thoughts away, memories of the event resurface with vivid clarity. The snapshot images of flames engulfing shelves and panicked coworkers seared into his brain like photographs on a wall. This guilt-ridden recollection makes him feel intensely ashamed – not just for surviving while others might have perished, but also because, in those initial moments, he thought only of himself. He recalls this selfishness with an acute sense of remorse, convinced that it somehow diminishes the trauma's reality and, by extension, his own worth. As Alejandro navigates his life as a retail worker once more, these triggers continue to wreak havoc on his daily routines. When coworkers engage in minor infractions like shoplifting or tardiness, he feels like he's reliving the event all over again – hence his growing reliance on magical thinking and physical self-harm. Suppressing memories becomes increasingly difficult when every misplaced item or careless customer seems to yank him back into that burning store. Alejandro tries to convince himself that these distractions will eventually quiet down, but so far, they've only intensified the flashbacks. His marriage has begun to fray at the seams as he withdraws from his wife's touch and conversation, fearing that speaking about the event might trigger more unwelcome memories or tempt him into more self-destructive habits. One particularly harrowing flashback finally brought Alejandro to seek help – on a crowded subway car during rush hour, when someone pushed against him with an elbow. He burst out of the train at the next stop and ran home in tears, overcome by shame and fear that this cycle would forever hold him hostage. With his wife's support, he hopes therapy can teach him new ways to break free from these triggers and find solace beyond the grip of the traumatic memories that haunt him still.
